Template: test-doc

Types: test-doc, test-case
Purpose: a test that is a document. Open it and the verdicts fill themselves in; point the command at it and a headless browser reads the same verdicts out of the same fields.
Behaviour: ./test.element.js, a classic script that runs every case in the page and writes what happened
Styling: ./test.template.css, plus the shared ../theme.css
Design: the spec, which carries the two venues this replaced and what it still cannot see

Why this template exists

The figure layout engine reads measured boxes for every decision it makes. Which edges share a connected component, how many lanes a gap needs, where a back edge's gutter runs — all of it comes from getBoundingClientRect.

happy-dom computes no layout, so the engine cannot be tested where validate already runs. Every rect comes back zero, which collapses every figure to one case and passes every check.

Two ways out looked plausible. Split the engine so its decisions take boxes and return lanes, then drive that with synthetic boxes. Or bring in a real browser and a test framework with it.

This is the third. The test is a document, the page runs itself, and a browser only opens it.

One page, two readers

A person opens the file and watches each test-status go from PENDING to SUCCESS or FAILURE. The command opens the same file in a headless browser, waits for the same fields to stop reading PENDING, and reads them out.

Nothing in the document knows which of the two is looking at it. That is the property worth having: the page a person debugs and the page a build gates on run identical code, so the two cannot drift.

Waiting on the statuses also carries asynchrony for free. A figure case waits for an animation frame and then for a ResizeObserver, and no case ever declares itself async or hands a promise to a harness.

PENDING is the only verdict a file may hold

test-status takes exactly one value on disk, and the schema says so. A result belongs to a run, not to the repository, and a committed SUCCESS is a claim somebody typed rather than something that happened.

The runner writes the other two words into the live page, where no validator ever looks. It mirrors each one into data-verdict at the same time, because CSS cannot select on text and the verdict has to stay in the text for a reader and the command to agree on it.

Two kinds of test, split by what they touch

A browser-test reaches a rendered page, and whether a person or the command opened that page changes nothing about it. A node-test reaches the filesystem and the command line. Both are the same document, and the type on a case's script says which one it is.

Nothing else declares the split, because a script type already carries exactly this meaning everywhere else here. mycelium/* marks a script that only ever loads under Node, so mycelium/test is a node case and text/mycelium-test is a browser one.

The split is about what a test touches rather than about what it needs to measure. An earlier framing divided them by whether a case needed real layout, which stopped meaning anything once a real browser became available.

One property does not carry across. A browser document is its own report, and a node document is not: nothing renders it, so its verdicts go to the command's output and never into the file.

What a node case gets

A node case exports one default function, receiving assert and a sandbox. Throwing fails the case, exactly as in a page.

The export carries no name because its position already says everything a name would. A script inside a test-case can only be that case's body, so naming it would repeat the tag above it. A command host exports a default for the same reason, so that mycelium validate does not read as mycelium validate validate.

The sandbox is a documents tree of its own, thrown away afterwards, with this repository's templates linked into it. sandbox.mycelium(…) runs the real command line against that tree and returns its output and exit status, and read, exists and write reach the files.

Spawning the real command costs more than calling the function would, and it buys what calling it would miss: how arguments parse, which path a command chooses, how a document serializes, and what exit code comes back.

Each case gets a fresh sandbox, so no test can see what another one wrote.

Shape

<test-doc data-conforms-to="../templates/test.template.html#test-doc">
  <test-title>The figure engine allocates lanes per channel</test-title>
  <test-subject><a href="../templates/figure.element.js">figure.element.js</a></test-subject>

  <test-case id="fork-shares-a-lane" data-conforms-to="../templates/test.template.html#test-case">
    <test-name>Two edges out of one node share a single lane</test-name>
    <test-status>PENDING</test-status>
    <test-fixture>
      <figure-graph data-columns="2">…</figure-graph>
    </test-fixture>
    <script type="text/mycelium-test">
      await settle(fixture)
      assert.near(laneOf(wires[0]), laneOf(wires[1]), 0.5, "the fork took two lanes")
    </script>
  </test-case>
</test-doc>

test-message holds why a case failed, and a document on disk carries none. The schema rejects an empty field, so the runner creates one at the moment it has something to put there.

test-fixture holds ordinary markup, live in the page rather than cloned into it. A figure inside one upgrades and draws exactly as it would anywhere else, which is the whole reason to write a test of markup in markup.

Why the case script is not a mycelium type

mycelium/* marks a script inside a document that only ever loads under Node, and that is exactly what lets one hold TypeScript. src/script-hooks.ts tells Node to strip types from any script carrying the prefix, and the editor reads the same prefix to decide it is looking at .ts.

A case script is the opposite. It runs in the browser, so it has to stay valid JavaScript, and giving it the prefix would let an author write a type annotation with a clean editor and a clean pnpm typecheck behind them. The failure arrives much later, as a syntax error inside the page, saying nothing about types.

So the type is text/mycelium-test. It sits outside the prefix, which keeps both tools treating it as JavaScript, and the browser skips it anyway because it does not recognise the type.

mycelium/test stays free for a node-test's script, where TypeScript is right and the prefix means what it says.

What a case script gets

A <script type="text/mycelium-test"> carries the body of the test. The browser skips it, and the runner evaluates it as the body of an async function.

Three names come in. fixture is the case's own test-fixture element, settle waits until an element stops changing, and assert throws when its first argument is false.

Throwing is the whole failure protocol. A case that returns has passed, and the message on whatever it threw lands in test-message.

assert.near compares two measured numbers with a tolerance. Geometry rarely lands on a whole number, so exact equality on anything a browser rounded is a flake waiting to happen.

Why the runner lives in the page

Putting it in the command instead would mean two implementations of what a case is: one the browser runs when a person opens the file, one the tool runs in CI. Those drift, and the drift shows up as a test that passes in one place and fails in the other.

So the command knows nothing about cases, fixtures or assertions. It opens a URL, waits for no field to read PENDING, and reads the fields. Everything else is the document's business.

test.element.js is a classic script and not a module, for the reason figure.template.html gives about file:// and the CORS check on module scripts.

How a run ends

The command sends the wait as an asynchronous script and lets the driver enforce the script timeout. Past the deadline a case still reading PENDING has failed, because a thrown error already writes FAILURE, so PENDING at the end means the script hung or the page never loaded its subject.

There is no TIMEOUT in the enum for the same reason. PENDING already means "nothing has answered", which is exactly what happened.

A page-level error short-circuits that wait. The runner listens for one, marks every case still reading PENDING as FAILURE, and puts the error in each message — so a missing subject script reports a reason rather than costing a full deadline.

The audits

Three checks, all reading the document rather than its rendering. A case carries a script, a browser document loads the page runner, and no document mixes the two kinds of case.

Each catches an authoring mistake whose only other symptom arrives late. A case with no script fails at run time, a browser document that never loads the runner leaves every case pending until the deadline, and a mixed document silently runs only half of itself while still reporting a complete result.

The command

run opens each test document in a headless browser and reports what the page decided. list prints what exists without running anything.

The driver provisions itself. Chrome for Testing publishes a chromedriver per platform as a plain zip, one per build number that an installed Chrome reports, so a first run downloads a matching driver and caches it. On a machine that already has one, CHROMEWEBDRIVER points at it and nothing downloads.

What this pass does not do

No authoring command. A test's substance is a fixture and a script, and neither fits on a flag, so writing one means writing the markup — the state figure is still in.

No second browser. WebDriver is the reason Firefox stays reachable, but nothing here asks for it yet.
